questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(20) · Meaning of a company
questions.stem: Which of the following is a 'company' within the meaning of section 2(20) of the Companies Act 2013?

readLink.label: Read: What a company is, s. 2(20) →

options.text: A corporation created by a special Act of Parliament to regulate a sector
options.explanation: A statutory corporation is a body corporate created by its own Act. It was never registered under any company law, so it fails the only test s. 2(20) sets.

options.text: A limited liability partnership registered under the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008
options.explanation: An LLP is a body corporate under its own statute and falls within s. 2(11), but it is not registered under a company law and so is not a company under s. 2(20).

options.text: An entity registered under the Companies Act 1956 and still carrying on business
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(20) covers a company incorporated under this Act OR under any previous company law, and the 1956 Act is a previous company law.

options.text: A multi-State co-operative society with paid-up capital of ₹ 12,00,00,000
options.explanation: A co-operative society is registered under co-operative legislation, not company law; s. 2(11) even excludes it from 'body corporate' expressly.

questions.stem: The expression 'body corporate' in section 2(11) of the Companies Act 2013:

options.text: Is narrower than 'company', because it covers only entities registered in India
options.explanation: This reverses the relationship. Body corporate is the wider expression and it expressly reaches entities incorporated outside India.

options.text: Includes a company incorporated outside India but excludes a co-operative society
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(11) says so in terms — it includes a company incorporated outside India, and excludes a co-operative society registered under any law relating to co-operative societies, plus any other body corporate the Central Government notifies.

options.text: Includes every co-operative society, since such a society has perpetual succession
options.explanation: Perpetual succession is not the test. The clause names co-operative societies as an exclusion regardless of their features.

options.text: Means the same thing as 'company' under s. 2(20)
options.explanation: Every company is a body corporate, but most bodies corporate — foreign companies, LLPs, statutory corporations — are not companies.

questions.stem: As the law stands on 28 February 2026, the position of the common seal of a company is that:

readLink.label: Read: The characteristics of a company →

options.text: Every company must have one, and every deed must be executed under it
options.explanation: This is the pre-2015 position. It is the commonest stale answer in this chapter.

options.text: Only a public company must have one; a private company need not
options.explanation: The amendment drew no distinction between private and public companies; the seal became optional for both.

options.text: It has been abolished, so no company may use a common seal at all
options.explanation: It was made optional, not abolished. A company may still adopt and use a seal if it wishes.

options.text: It is optional, and where a company has none, documents are signed by two directors, or by one director and the company secretary where one is appointed
options.explanation: Correct. The Companies (Amendment) Act 2015 made the seal optional and supplied exactly this signing alternative, which is why the seal is no longer listed as a characteristic of a company.

questions.stem: All seven members of a public company die in a single accident. The legal position of the company is that:

readLink.label: Read: The characteristics of a company →

options.text: It continues in existence, the shares vesting in the legal representatives of the deceased members
options.explanation: Correct. Perpetual succession means the company's existence is unaffected by the death, insolvency or exit of members; only the register of members changes.

options.text: It stands automatically dissolved on the death of the last member
options.explanation: Nothing in the Act dissolves a company on the death of its members. Dissolution follows winding up or striking off.

options.text: It becomes a One Person Company in the hands of the senior-most legal representative
options.explanation: An OPC is formed as such under s. 3(1)(c); a public company does not convert into one by operation of law on a death.

options.text: Its contracts lapse, because the persons who made them are dead
options.explanation: The contracts were made by the company, a separate person, not by the members. The company's death has not occurred, so its contracts stand.

questions.stem: Rukmini holds 98 per cent of the shares of a private company that owns a warehouse. She insures the warehouse in her own name. On a fire, the insurer repudiates the claim. The insurer is:

readLink.label: Read: The characteristics of a company →

options.text: Wrong, because a 98 per cent shareholder is in substance the owner of the company's assets
options.explanation: Substance is exactly what separate personality refuses to look at. Shareholding is not ownership of the company's individual assets.

options.text: Wrong, because the company would have been entitled to claim and she may claim on its behalf
options.explanation: A member has no authority, merely as a member, to act for the company; and the policy here is in her own name, not the company's.

options.text: Right, because the warehouse belongs to the company and she has no insurable interest in it
options.explanation: Correct. The company's property is the company's, not the members' proportionately, so even a 98 per cent shareholder has no insurable interest in a particular company asset.

options.text: Right, but only because she did not disclose her shareholding when taking the policy
options.explanation: Non-disclosure is a different defence altogether. The claim fails at the earlier point of insurable interest, whatever was disclosed.

questions.stem: Describing a company as an 'artificial legal person' means that:

readLink.label: Read: The characteristics of a company →

options.text: Its legal personality is a pretence which the courts disregard whenever it is convenient
options.explanation: The personality is real in law. Courts disregard it only on a recognised ground for lifting the veil, and never merely for convenience.

options.text: It has legal personality created by law but no physical existence, so it acts only through natural persons
options.explanation: Correct. The company is a person in the eye of the law with no body, no mind of its own and no capacity to appear in person; the Board, officers and agents act for it.

options.text: It enjoys every right a natural person enjoys, including the right to vote in an election
options.explanation: A company holds only those rights compatible with an artificial person; personal and political rights of citizenship are not among them.

options.text: It cannot commit any wrong, because a wrong requires a human mind
options.explanation: A company can be liable in tort and, in many cases, criminally; the acts and intentions of those who control it are attributed to it.

questions.stem: The proposition established by Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd is that:
questions.sourceRef: s. 9; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd

readLink.label: Read: Separate legal entity in action →

options.text: A duly incorporated company is a person distinct from its members, and is not their agent or trustee however few they are
options.explanation: Correct. That is why the founder ranked as a secured creditor of the company he had formed and controlled, ahead of the unsecured trade creditors.

options.text: A member holding almost all the shares becomes personally liable for the company's debts
options.explanation: This is the argument the creditors made and lost. Concentrated shareholding is not a ground for personal liability.

options.text: A company cannot lend to, or borrow from, its own controlling shareholder
options.explanation: Nothing in the case bars such dealings; the whole point was that the company's dealings with its controller were valid.

options.text: The corporate veil is lifted wherever a company is controlled by one family
options.explanation: The opposite. The case is the leading authority for refusing to lift the veil in exactly that situation.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Separate legal entity · Lee v Lee's Air Farming
questions.stem: Ilango holds all but one share of a private company, is its sole director, and is also employed by it as its chief engineer under a written contract of service. He is injured at work and claims compensation as an employee. His claim:
questions.sourceRef: s. 9; Lee v Lee's Air Farming Ltd

readLink.label: Read: Separate legal entity in action →

options.text: Fails, because a person cannot contract with himself
options.explanation: He is not contracting with himself. The contract is between him and the company, which is a different person in law.

options.text: Fails, because a sole director is the alter ego of the company
options.explanation: The 'alter ego' idea is used to attribute acts to a company, not to destroy a contract of employment between the company and an individual.

options.text: Succeeds only if the company had obtained an insurance policy naming him
options.explanation: The existence of a policy affects who pays, not whether he is an employee. His status comes from the contract of service.

options.text: Succeeds, because the company and he are two distinct persons and the contract of service between them is valid
options.explanation: Correct. This is the Lee v Lee's Air Farming point: one person may at the same time be the controlling shareholder, the sole director and an employee of the company.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 3A · Statutory lifting of the veil
questions.stem: The membership of a private company falls to one on 5 January 2026. The company continues to trade and on 2 October 2026 contracts an unsecured debt. Under section 3A:

options.text: The company stands dissolved from 5 July 2026 and the debt is unenforceable
options.explanation: Section 3A does not dissolve the company. It continues to exist and to be liable; only the member's shield is withdrawn.

options.text: The sole member is liable for the debt from the moment the membership fell below two
options.explanation: Liability attaches only for debts contracted after the company has traded for MORE than six months while so reduced, not from the moment of the shortfall.

options.text: The member, if cognisant of the fact, is severally liable for the whole of that debt, the six months having expired on 5 July 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3A engages after six months of trading below the minimum, catches only members cognisant of the fact, and makes them severally liable for the whole of the debts contracted during that time.

options.text: The member is jointly liable with the company for half the debt
options.explanation: The section makes the liability several and for the whole of the debt, not joint and not proportionate.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Lifting the veil · Evading an existing obligation
questions.stem: Having agreed in writing to sell his factory land to Tanmay, Sudarshan instead transfers it to a company he forms and wholly owns, so as to defeat Tanmay's suit for specific performance. The court will most likely:
questions.sourceRef: Jones v Lipman; Gilford Motor Co v Horne

options.text: Refuse relief against the company, since it was not a party to the agreement, and leave Tanmay to damages
options.explanation: That is the answer where the company is genuine. Here the company was created to defeat an obligation already binding on its controller, which is the classic ground for looking through it.

options.text: Treat the company as a mere device or façade for Sudarshan and decree specific performance against both
options.explanation: Correct. This is the Jones v Lipman pattern, the same reasoning applied in Gilford Motor Co v Horne to a restrictive covenant: a company formed to escape a pre-existing obligation is looked through.

options.text: Order the company to be wound up, that being the only remedy against a sham company
options.explanation: Winding up is not the remedy for this. Lifting the veil produces liability or an order against the persons behind the company, not its dissolution.

options.text: Hold the transfer valid, because a company is a separate legal person and may buy land from anyone
options.explanation: This states the rule without asking whether an exception applies. The fact that the company was formed after the obligation arose, to defeat it, is the exception.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Lifting the veil · What is NOT a ground
questions.stem: Which of the following, standing alone, is NOT a ground for lifting the corporate veil?

options.text: Incorporation obtained by furnishing false or incorrect information
options.explanation: This is an express statutory ground under s. 7(7), on which the Tribunal may even make the members' liability unlimited.

options.text: Carrying on the business of the company with intent to defraud creditors
options.explanation: Section 339 lets the Tribunal declare the persons knowingly party to it personally liable without any limitation of liability.

options.text: Formation of the company purely to reduce the tax payable by its controller, the income returning to him as loans
options.explanation: That is the Sir Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit ground — protection of revenue — and the courts disregard the company for that purpose.

options.text: The fact that one shareholder holds virtually all the shares and the company has since become insolvent
options.explanation: Correct. This is Salomon on its own facts. Concentrated ownership plus commercial failure is not fraud, and neither is a ground for piercing.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Lifting the veil · Enemy character
questions.stem: A company registered in India is controlled entirely by persons resident in a country at war with India. In deciding whether the company may trade with an Indian party, a court applying the reasoning in Daimler Co Ltd v Continental Tyre & Rubber Co would:
questions.sourceRef: Daimler Co Ltd v Continental Tyre & Rubber Co

options.text: Look at the nationality and residence of the persons in control and may treat the company as an enemy
options.explanation: Correct. A company has no nationality of its own in the ordinary sense, so for the limited purpose of trading with the enemy the court looks at who controls it.

options.text: Look only at the place of registration, which conclusively fixes the company's character
options.explanation: That is the general rule, and it is exactly what the case departs from where enemy character is in issue.

options.text: Treat the question as one of company law only, so the company's trading is unaffected
options.explanation: The doctrine exists precisely because a rule of company law would otherwise defeat a rule of public policy in wartime.

options.text: Hold that the company has automatically ceased to exist on the outbreak of hostilities
options.explanation: The company continues to exist. What is affected is its capacity to trade, by attributing enemy character to it.

questions.stem: Classifying companies on the basis of incorporation, the Life Insurance Corporation of India is:

readLink.label: Read: Classification on the basis of incorporation →

options.text: A chartered company, because it was set up by an instrument of the sovereign
options.explanation: Chartered companies are created by Royal Charter and are of historical interest only; none exists in India today.

options.text: A statutory company, created by a special Act and therefore a body corporate but not a 'company' under s. 2(20)
options.explanation: Correct. It owes its existence to its own Act, is governed primarily by that Act, and was never registered under any company law.

options.text: A registered company, because it is registered with the Registrar of Companies
options.explanation: A registered company comes into existence on registration under the Companies Act. A statutory corporation exists from the day its Act commences.

options.text: A Government company, since the Central Government controls it
options.explanation: A Government company under s. 2(45) must first be a company — that is, registered under company law — with 51 per cent or more of its paid-up capital held by Government.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(21) · Company limited by guarantee
questions.stem: A company limited by guarantee, whose members have each undertaken to contribute ₹ 25,000, runs short of working capital while trading normally. It calls on the members to pay the guaranteed amount. The members:

readLink.label: Read: Classification on the basis of liability →

options.text: Must pay, because the guarantee is a present debt owed to the company
options.explanation: The guarantee is not a present debt. It is an undertaking to contribute in a future contingency, and until that contingency arrives nothing is payable.

options.text: Must pay, but only to the extent the company is unable to meet its liabilities out of its own funds
options.explanation: That is a test of amount, not of timing. The obstacle is that the event which makes the guarantee payable has not occurred at all.

options.text: Need not pay, because the guaranteed amount is contributable only in the event of winding up
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(21) fixes the members' liability at the amount they undertake to contribute to the assets of the company 'in the event of its being wound up', so the call is premature.

options.text: Need not pay, because a guarantee company cannot have any share capital
options.explanation: A guarantee company may or may not have share capital; where it has, a member owes the unpaid amount on his shares in addition to the guarantee.

questions.stem: In an unlimited company registered under the Companies Act 2013, a trade creditor whose bill is unpaid:

readLink.label: Read: Classification on the basis of liability →

options.text: Must sue the company, the members' unlimited liability being enforced through the liquidator in a winding up
options.explanation: Correct. Unlimited liability removes the cap on what members must contribute, but it does not abolish the company's separate personality; the creditor's contract is with the company.

options.text: May sue any member directly, because the members have no limit on their liability
options.explanation: This confuses the amount of the liability with the person against whom it is enforced. The company remains a distinct legal person and the proper defendant.

options.text: May sue the directors, who alone bear unlimited liability in such a company
options.explanation: The unlimited liability in s. 2(92) is that of the members, not of the directors as such.

options.text: Cannot recover at all, since an unlimited company is not a body corporate
options.explanation: An unlimited company is registered under the Act and is fully a body corporate with all the incidents of incorporation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three restrictions a private company must contain in its articles under section 2(68)?

options.text: A restriction on the right to transfer its shares
options.explanation: This is the first restriction the clause requires, and it must be in the articles.

options.text: A limit of two hundred on the number of its members
options.explanation: This is the second restriction, subject to the joint-holder and employee counting rules and disapplied for a One Person Company.

options.text: A prohibition on any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities
options.explanation: This is the third restriction, and it is what keeps a private company outside the prospectus machinery.

options.text: A minimum paid-up share capital of ₹ 1,00,000
options.explanation: Correct. This is what the clause no longer requires. The fixed figure was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015 and nothing has been prescribed since.

questions.stem: The register of members of Kalyani Weaves Private Limited shows: 96 individuals holding shares in their own names, none of them employees; 21 shareholdings each held jointly by 2 persons, none of whom appears elsewhere on the register; 34 current employees of the company who hold shares; 5 former employees who became members while in employment and have continued as members since leaving; and 48 debenture-holders. For the purposes of section 2(68)(ii), the number of members is:

options.explanation: Correct. 96 individuals plus 21 joint holdings counted as one member each = 117. The 34 current employees and the 5 qualifying ex-employees are excluded, and debenture-holders are not members at all.
This applies the employee exclusions but counts each of the 42 joint holders separately (96 + 42), ignoring the rule that joint holders are a single member.
This is the raw head-count of every person on the register of members (96 + 42 + 34 + 5), applying neither of the two provisos.
This adds the 48 debenture-holders to the raw head-count. Debenture-holders are creditors, never members, and never enter the calculation.

questions.stem: Which of the following persons IS counted towards the two-hundred-member limit of a private company?

options.text: A store supervisor presently employed by the company who holds 400 shares
options.explanation: A person in the employment of the company is excluded by the first limb of the second proviso, whatever the size of his holding.

options.text: A retired accountant who bought his shares three years after resigning from the company
options.explanation: Correct. The ex-employee exclusion needs the person to have become a member WHILE in the employment. Buying in after leaving fails that condition, so he counts.

options.text: A retired foreman who acquired his shares while employed and has kept them since retiring
options.explanation: He satisfies all three conditions of the exclusion — employed, a member while employed, and still a member — so he is not counted.

options.text: A bank holding 5,000 debentures of the company
options.explanation: A debenture-holder is a creditor of the company, not a member, and never enters the count at all.

questions.stem: On the position as on 28 February 2026, the minimum paid-up share capital required for a private company is:

options.explanation: This was the figure written into the clause as originally enacted. It was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015.
₹ 5,00,000 was the corresponding figure for a public company, and it too was omitted in 2015.

options.text: Nil — the clause now reads 'such minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed', and nothing has been prescribed
options.explanation: Correct. Both the private-company and public-company minimums were removed in 2015 and no amount stands prescribed, so there is no minimum today.

options.text: ₹ 1,00,000, but only for a private company that is a subsidiary of a public company
options.explanation: The deemed-public proviso to s. 2(71) changes such a company's classification; it does not revive a capital requirement that no longer exists.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(71) proviso · Deemed public company
questions.stem: Harita Ceramics Limited, an unlisted public company, holds 68 per cent of the total voting power of Sunetra Tiles Private Limited, whose articles restrict transfer, cap members at 200 and bar invitations to the public. Sunetra has 34 members. For the purposes of the Companies Act 2013, Sunetra is:

options.text: A private company, because its articles contain all three restrictions
options.explanation: Its articles do keep it private in form, and the proviso to s. 2(71) applies notwithstanding exactly that.

options.text: A private company, because it has only 34 members, far below the cap of 200
options.explanation: Size is irrelevant to the deeming. What matters is the identity of the company that controls it.

options.text: A public company, but only if it first alters its articles and changes its name
options.explanation: The deeming operates by force of the proviso. No alteration of articles or of name is needed, and the name may lawfully continue to end in 'Private Limited'.

options.text: A public company, being a subsidiary of a company which is not a private company, even though it continues to be a private company in its articles
options.explanation: Correct. Harita controls more than one-half of Sunetra's voting power, so Sunetra is its subsidiary under s. 2(87)(ii); Harita is not a private company, so the proviso to s. 2(71) deems Sunetra public.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts a private company with a public company under the Companies Act 2013?

options.text: A private company needs two subscribers and two directors; a public company needs seven subscribers and three directors
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3(1) fixes two and seven subscribers respectively, and the minimum number of directors is two for a private company and three for a public one.

options.text: A private company needs seven subscribers and a public company two, the numbers being reversed by the 2015 amendment
options.explanation: The numbers are the other way round and the 2015 amendment did not touch them; it removed the minimum capital requirements.

options.text: Shares of a private company are freely transferable while those of a public company are not
options.explanation: This inverts the position. A private company's articles must RESTRICT transfer; a public company's shares are freely transferable.

options.text: A public company is capped at two hundred members and a private company has no cap
options.explanation: The cap of two hundred applies to a private company; a public company has no maximum number of members.

questions.stem: The nominee named in the memorandum of a One Person Company:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(62) with the Explanation to s. 3(1)

options.text: Is a second member of the company, so that an OPC in fact has two members
options.explanation: If the OPC had two members it would cease to answer s. 2(62), which requires only one person as a member. The nominee holds nothing while the member lives.

options.text: May be named without his knowledge, his consent being required only when he actually becomes a member
options.explanation: The consent must be obtained in writing BEFORE the name is entered and filed with the Registrar at incorporation.

options.text: Becomes the member on the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract, his prior written consent having been filed with the Registrar
options.explanation: Correct. The nominee is a successor in waiting: he is not a member while the subscriber lives, his prior written consent is mandatory, and the member may change him or he may withdraw on intimation to the Registrar.

options.text: Cannot be changed once named, since the memorandum is the company's charter
options.explanation: The member may change the nominee at any time, and the nominee may himself withdraw; each change is intimated to the Registrar.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(62) · Status of an OPC
questions.stem: Which statement about a One Person Company is correct?

options.text: It is a fourth class of company, standing outside the private-public classification
options.explanation: It is a species of private company, formed as such under s. 3(1)(c), and its name carries '(OPC) Private Limited'.

options.text: It is a private company, and the two-hundred-member limb of s. 2(68) is expressly disapplied to it
options.explanation: Correct. An OPC is formed as a private company and the membership cap could never engage a company with exactly one member, so the clause disapplies that limb in terms.

options.text: It must hold an annual general meeting like any other private company
options.explanation: An OPC is relieved of the requirement to hold an annual general meeting — one of the relaxations that make the form attractive.

options.text: It can never be a small company, because it has only one member
options.explanation: Small-company status turns on not being a public company, the two thresholds and the three exclusions. An OPC that satisfies them is a small company; the two labels are independent.

questions.stem: Charukesha Fabrics Private Limited has paid-up share capital of ₹ 3,20,00,000 and turnover, as per the profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year, of ₹ 44,00,00,000. It is neither a holding nor a subsidiary company, is not registered under section 8, and is not governed by any special Act. On the position as on 28 February 2026 it is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(85) with the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules

options.text: A small company, its paid-up share capital being within the prescribed limit of ₹ 4,00,00,000
options.explanation: The capital limb is satisfied, but s. 2(85) requires BOTH limbs. Satisfying one is not enough.

options.text: A small company, because the two limbs are alternatives and only one need be satisfied
options.explanation: The clause joins the limbs with 'and'. They are cumulative, not alternative.

options.text: Not a small company, because a private company can never be a small company
options.explanation: This reverses the clause. Small-company status is confined to companies OTHER THAN public companies, so a private company is the usual candidate for it.

options.text: Not a small company, because turnover of ₹ 44,00,00,000 exceeds the prescribed limit of ₹ 40,00,00,000 and both limbs must be satisfied
options.explanation: Correct. Capital of ₹ 3,20,00,000 is within ₹ 4,00,00,000, but turnover of ₹ 44,00,00,000 exceeds ₹ 40,00,00,000, and the two tests are cumulative.

questions.stem: A private company has paid-up share capital of ₹ 2,00,000, no turnover at all, and is a wholly-owned subsidiary of another private company. It is:

options.text: Not a small company, because a subsidiary company is excluded outright whatever its size
options.explanation: Correct. Exclusion (A) in s. 2(85) removes a holding company and a subsidiary company from the clause altogether, and the exclusions are checked before any arithmetic.

options.text: A small company, both thresholds being satisfied by a wide margin
options.explanation: The thresholds are satisfied, but the clause never reaches them for an excluded company.

options.text: A small company, because the exclusion applies only where the holding company is a public company
options.explanation: The exclusion is unqualified. It does not ask what kind of company the holding company is.

options.text: Not a small company, because a company with no turnover cannot satisfy the turnover test
options.explanation: Nil turnover comfortably 'does not exceed' the prescribed amount, so the turnover limb passes. The company fails for a different reason.

questions.stem: For the turnover test in section 2(85), the turnover to be looked at is that:

options.text: Estimated for the current financial year on the basis of the management's projections
options.explanation: A projection is not a figure 'as per the profit and loss account', and the clause fixes a completed year deliberately so that status is certain.

options.text: Averaged over the three immediately preceding financial years
options.explanation: Averaging appears in some Rules made under the Act at other times, but the small-company clause looks at a single year.

options.text: As per the profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the words of the clause, and they make status depend on an audited figure for a completed year rather than on a moving estimate.

options.text: As per the profit and loss account for the financial year in which the question arises
options.explanation: The current year's account does not exist while the year is running, which is precisely why the clause points to the immediately preceding year.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(87)(ii) · Voting power, not capital
questions.stem: Sharavati Limited has issued 9,00,000 equity shares of ₹ 10 each carrying one vote per share, and 6,00,000 preference shares of ₹ 10 each which carry no voting rights except on resolutions directly affecting them. Netravati Limited holds 4,05,000 equity shares and all 6,00,000 preference shares. Sharavati Limited is:

options.text: A subsidiary of Netravati Limited, which holds 67 per cent of its paid-up share capital
options.explanation: 67 per cent is the paid-up-capital figure (₹ 1,00,50,000 of ₹ 1,50,00,000). Since the 2017 amendment s. 2(87)(ii) has run on total voting power, and this figure is the distractor built from the discarded base.

options.text: An associate of Netravati Limited, which controls 45 per cent of its total voting power
options.explanation: Correct. Total voting power is 9,00,000 votes; Netravati controls 4,05,000, that is 45 per cent. That is not more than one-half, so the subsidiary test fails, but it is at least 20 per cent, so s. 2(6) makes it an associate.

options.text: A subsidiary of Netravati Limited, preference shares carrying votes on every resolution
options.explanation: Preference shares of this description carry votes only on resolutions directly affecting them, so they do not enter the general voting base.

options.text: Neither a subsidiary nor an associate, 45 per cent being less than one-half
options.explanation: Failing the subsidiary test is only the first step. Significant influence under s. 2(6) needs at least 20 per cent, and 45 per cent clears it.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(87) Explanation · Control through a subsidiary
questions.stem: Marudhar Limited controls 54 per cent of the total voting power of Nalanda Limited. Nalanda Limited controls 51 per cent of the total voting power of Palamau Limited. Marudhar Limited holds no shares at all in Palamau Limited and has no agreement with it. In relation to Marudhar Limited, Palamau Limited is:

options.text: An associate, Marudhar's effective interest being 54 per cent of 51 per cent, that is 27.54 per cent
options.explanation: Percentages are never multiplied down a chain under s. 2(87). The 27.54 per cent figure has no place in the clause and exists only as a trap.

options.text: Unconnected with Marudhar Limited, which holds no shares in it
options.explanation: Direct shareholding is not required. The Explanation deems a company a subsidiary of the holding company even where the control is exercised by another subsidiary.

options.text: A subsidiary of Nalanda Limited alone, the chain having no effect further up
options.explanation: It is certainly a subsidiary of Nalanda, but the Explanation carries the relationship up the chain to Marudhar as well.

options.text: A subsidiary of Nalanda Limited and also a subsidiary of Marudhar Limited, control exercised through another subsidiary being sufficient
options.explanation: Correct. Nalanda controls more than one-half of Palamau's voting power, and Nalanda is itself Marudhar's subsidiary, so the Explanation to s. 2(87) makes Palamau a subsidiary of Marudhar too.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(6) · The twenty per cent boundary
questions.stem: Vaigai Limited holds 3,00,000 of the 15,00,000 equity shares of Wainganga Limited, each share carrying one vote. Wainganga has issued no other voting securities, and there is no agreement between the two companies about Wainganga's business decisions. Wainganga Limited is:

options.text: An associate of Vaigai Limited, significant influence being control of at least twenty per cent of total voting power
options.explanation: Correct. 3,00,000 of 15,00,000 votes is exactly 20.00 per cent, and the clause says 'at least twenty per cent', so the boundary is inclusive and the relationship is made out.

options.text: A subsidiary of Vaigai Limited
options.explanation: The subsidiary test needs control of the Board's composition or of MORE THAN one-half of total voting power. Twenty per cent is neither.

options.text: Neither a subsidiary nor an associate, because s. 2(6) requires more than twenty per cent
options.explanation: The clause reads 'at least twenty per cent', deliberately different from the 'more than one-half' comparator in s. 2(87)(ii). Exactly twenty per cent qualifies.

options.text: A joint venture of Vaigai Limited
options.explanation: A joint venture requires a joint arrangement in which the parties have joint control and rights to the net assets. A bare 20 per cent shareholding is not that.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(87)(i) · Control of Board composition
questions.stem: Under an agreement recorded in its articles, Ashtavinayak Limited may appoint 5 of the 9 directors of Bharani Limited but holds only 4 per cent of Bharani's equity shares. Bharani Limited is:

options.text: Not a subsidiary, because a 4 per cent holding cannot amount to control
options.explanation: Limb (i) of s. 2(87) has nothing to do with shareholding. A company holding no shares at all can control the composition of another's Board.

options.text: An associate, because the right to appoint directors is participation in business decisions under an agreement
options.explanation: Section 2(6) excludes a subsidiary expressly, and the subsidiary test must be run first. Here it succeeds, so the associate question never arises.

options.text: A subsidiary of Ashtavinayak Limited, which controls the composition of its Board of Directors
options.explanation: Correct. The power to appoint a majority of the directors — 5 of 9 — is control of the composition of the Board, and limb (i) of s. 2(87) is satisfied on its own.

options.text: A subsidiary only if Ashtavinayak also acquires more than one-half of its total voting power
options.explanation: The two limbs of s. 2(87) are alternatives joined by 'or'. Either one alone is enough.

questions.stem: Which statement about the relationship between section 2(6) and section 2(87) is correct?

options.text: A company may be a subsidiary and an associate of the same company at the same time
options.explanation: Section 2(6) excludes a subsidiary in terms — an associate is a company in which there is significant influence 'but which is not a subsidiary'.

options.text: Both clauses use the same comparator, namely 'not less than' the stated percentage
options.explanation: The comparators are deliberately different: 'more than one-half' in s. 2(87)(ii), 'at least twenty per cent' in the Explanation to s. 2(6).

options.text: Section 2(6) is tested first, and only if significant influence is absent does one ask about subsidiary status
options.explanation: The order is the other way round, because the associate definition itself is subject to the company not being a subsidiary.

options.text: Subsidiary status is tested first, and associate status arises only if the subsidiary test fails; the comparators are 'more than one-half' and 'at least twenty per cent' respectively
options.explanation: Correct. The words 'but which is not a subsidiary' fix the order of the tests, and the two clauses use different comparators — one exclusive, the other inclusive.

questions.stem: Kolar Minerals Limited has paid-up share capital of ₹ 80,00,00,000, of which the Central Government holds ₹ 18,00,00,000, the Government of Karnataka ₹ 15,00,00,000 and the Government of Telangana ₹ 9,00,00,000; the balance is held by the public. Kolar Minerals Limited is:

options.text: Not a Government company, because no single Government holds not less than 51 per cent
options.explanation: The clause covers a holding partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments, so the holdings are aggregated and no single Government need reach the threshold.

options.text: A Government company, the aggregate Government holding being ₹ 42,00,00,000, that is 52.5 per cent of the paid-up share capital
options.explanation: Correct. ₹ 18,00,00,000 + ₹ 15,00,00,000 + ₹ 9,00,00,000 = ₹ 42,00,00,000 on a base of ₹ 80,00,00,000, which is 52.5 per cent — not less than the 51 per cent s. 2(45) requires.

options.text: Not a Government company, because only the Central Government's holding of 22.5 per cent counts
options.explanation: The clause names State Governments expressly, both alone and in combination with the Centre.

options.text: A Government company only if the three Governments together also control more than one-half of the total voting power
options.explanation: Section 2(45) is one of the few control definitions that runs on PAID-UP SHARE CAPITAL. The voting-power base belongs to s. 2(87)(ii).

questions.stem: Zenith Optics Pte Ltd is incorporated in Singapore. It maintains a liaison office in Chennai which only collects market information and does no business, and it makes no sales into India. Zenith Optics Pte Ltd is:

options.text: Not a foreign company, because s. 2(42) requires a place of business in India AND the conduct of business activity in India
options.explanation: Correct. The two limbs are joined by 'and'. A place of business without business activity, like this liaison office, does not satisfy the clause.

options.text: A foreign company, because it has a place of business in India
options.explanation: This reads the clause with 'or'. Limb (a) alone is not enough; limb (b) requires business activity in India as well.

options.text: A foreign company, because any company incorporated outside India is a foreign company for the Act
options.explanation: Incorporation outside India is only the threshold. Both further limbs must then be satisfied.

options.text: Not a foreign company, because the clause applies only to companies and not to bodies corporate
options.explanation: The clause says 'any company or body corporate incorporated outside India', so a foreign body corporate that is not a company is within it.

questions.stem: A public company's equity shares are unlisted, but its non-convertible debentures are listed on a recognised stock exchange. Applying the main part of section 2(52), the company is prima facie:

options.text: Not a listed company, because only an equity listing counts
options.explanation: The clause speaks of 'any of its securities', which is wider than equity shares.

options.text: Not a listed company, because debentures are a borrowing and not a security
options.explanation: Debentures are securities. The word covers shares, debentures and the other instruments named in the definition of 'securities'.

options.text: A listed company only if the debentures were issued to the public rather than privately placed
options.explanation: The mode of issue matters only under the proviso and the carve-out Rules. The main part of the clause asks simply whether any securities are listed.

options.text: A listed company, since the clause covers a company which has any of its securities listed on a recognised stock exchange
options.explanation: Correct. On the main part of s. 2(52) a debenture listing makes the company listed; a proviso allows the Central Government to prescribe carve-outs, and that Rules-level list is Intermediate-level detail.

questions.stem: A society promoting research in soil science applies for registration as a section 8 company. It expects to earn a surplus from consultancy work, which it proposes to spend entirely on research, and it does not propose to pay any dividend. The application:

options.text: Must fail, because a section 8 company is forbidden to earn any profit
options.explanation: Nothing in s. 8 forbids earning a profit. The prohibition is on distributing it.

options.text: Must fail, because research is not one of the objects named in s. 8(1)(a)
options.explanation: Research is named expressly in the list, along with commerce, art, science, sports, education, social welfare, religion, charity and protection of the environment.

options.text: May succeed, because a section 8 company may earn profits provided it applies them only to its objects and prohibits any dividend
options.explanation: Correct. All three conditions of s. 8(1) are met: a listed object, an intention to apply income only to that object, and a prohibition on the payment of any dividend to members.

options.text: May succeed only if the company is registered as an unlimited company
options.explanation: A s. 8 company is registered as a limited company — usually limited by guarantee — and simply drops 'Limited' or 'Private Limited' from its name.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 8 · Incidents of a section 8 company
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT correct about a company registered under section 8?

options.text: A firm may be a member of it
options.explanation: This is correct and is an express exception in s. 8(3), notable because a firm is not otherwise a person that can hold shares in its own name.

options.text: Its members may alter its memorandum and articles by special resolution alone
options.explanation: Correct. This is the incorrect statement, and therefore the answer: s. 8(4)(i) allows alteration of the memorandum or articles only with the previous approval of the Central Government, because the licence rests on the constitution as approved.

options.text: It can never be a small company, whatever its capital or turnover
options.explanation: This is correct: exclusion (B) in s. 2(85) removes a s. 8 company from the small-company clause outright.

options.text: Its licence may be revoked by the Central Government after notice and an opportunity of being heard
options.explanation: This is correct: s. 8(6) allows revocation for contravention or for affairs conducted fraudulently, against the objects or prejudicially to the public interest, after a hearing.

questions.stem: A company registered in 2025 to hold a plot of land for a project starting in 2029 has made no payments except the Registrar's fees and the cost of maintaining its office and records. To obtain the status of a dormant company it:

readLink.label: Read: Dormant, Nidhi and producer companies →

options.text: Must apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, the payments made being expressly outside the meaning of a significant accounting transaction
options.explanation: Correct. Dormancy is a status applied for and entered in the register of dormant companies; and payments of fees to the Registrar and for maintaining the office and records are expressly excluded from 'significant accounting transaction'.

options.text: Need do nothing, since the status attaches automatically to any company with no business
options.explanation: There is no automatic dormancy. The Registrar acts on an application and maintains a register of dormant companies.

options.text: Is disqualified, because payments of fees to the Registrar are significant accounting transactions
options.explanation: The Explanation excludes exactly those payments, together with payments to fulfil the requirements of the Act, allotments to fulfil such requirements, and office and record maintenance.

options.text: Must first convert itself into a section 8 company
options.explanation: Dormancy has nothing to do with charitable objects. A company of any class may seek the status if it meets s. 455.

questions.stem: Which statement about a producer company is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Dormant, Nidhi and producer companies →

options.text: It may be formed by any seven persons, whether or not they are producers
options.explanation: Seven is the figure for an ordinary public company. A producer company needs producers, and its membership is confined to them.

options.text: Its shares are freely transferable, like those of a public company
options.explanation: Its shares are not freely transferable; a transfer needs the approval of the Board and can be made only to another active member.

options.text: It is treated as a public company, so the limit of two hundred members does not apply to it
options.explanation: The 200-member cap indeed does not apply, but the reason is wrong: a producer company is treated as a PRIVATE company under the Act.

options.text: It may be formed by ten or more individuals each of whom is a producer, or by two or more producer institutions, and is treated as a private company without the two-hundred-member cap
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the formation requirements, and although a producer company is treated as a private company it is expressly relieved of the membership cap so that large groups of producers can join.

questions.stem: The defining feature of a Nidhi company under section 406 is that it:

readLink.label: Read: Dormant, Nidhi and producer companies →

options.text: Is licensed by the Central Government to apply its profits only to charitable objects
options.explanation: That is the section 8 company. A Nidhi is an ordinary profit-making company serving its own members.

options.text: Accepts deposits from the public at large but lends only to its members
options.explanation: A Nidhi neither takes deposits from nor lends to anyone outside its membership. Both sides of its business are confined to members.

options.text: Is incorporated to cultivate the habit of thrift and savings among its members, receiving deposits from and lending to its members only, for their mutual benefit
options.explanation: Correct. That is the substance of s. 406, and the words 'members only' are the whole point of the class; a Nidhi is a public company and carries 'Nidhi Limited' in its name.

options.text: Is a private company formed by ten or more individual depositors
options.explanation: A Nidhi is a public company limited by shares; the ten-or-more-individuals formation rule belongs to producer companies.

questions.stem: Under section 3(1) of the Companies Act 2013, the minimum number of persons who must subscribe to the memorandum for a public company, a private company and a One Person Company respectively is:

readLink.label: Read: Formation of a company, s. 3 →

options.text: Two, seven and one
options.explanation: The first two figures are the wrong way round: seven is for a public company and two for a private one.

options.text: Seven, two and one
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3(1)(a) requires seven or more persons for a public company, s. 3(1)(b) two or more for a private company, and s. 3(1)(c) one person for a One Person Company.

options.text: Seven, three and one
options.explanation: Three is the minimum number of DIRECTORS of a public company, not the minimum number of subscribers to a private company's memorandum.

options.text: Ten, two and one
options.explanation: Ten is the minimum number of individual producers who may form a producer company, not the figure for a public company.

questions.stem: Which statement about the memorandum and the articles of association is correct?

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum and the articles →

options.text: The memorandum defines the company's capacity and prevails over the articles, while the Act prevails over both
options.explanation: Correct. Section 6 makes the Act override the memorandum, the articles, any agreement and any resolution, and the articles are in turn subordinate to the memorandum.

options.text: The articles prevail over the memorandum, being the more detailed document
options.explanation: Detail does not confer authority. The articles are the internal regulations and are subordinate to the memorandum.

options.text: The registered office clause of the memorandum must state the full postal address of the office
options.explanation: It states only the STATE in which the registered office is to be situated; the address is notified separately under s. 12.

options.text: A company registered after the commencement of the Act must adopt the model articles in Schedule I without modification
options.explanation: The model articles apply only to the extent the company's own registered articles do not exclude or modify them.

questions.stem: A promoter signs a contract with a machinery supplier 'for and on behalf of' a company that has not yet been incorporated. After incorporation the Board passes a resolution ratifying the contract. The position is that:

options.text: The company is bound from the date of the contract, the ratification relating back to that date
options.explanation: Relation back is the effect of a valid ratification. Ratification is impossible here because the company did not exist when the contract was made.

options.text: The company is bound from the date of incorporation, since a company may ratify any act done in its name
options.explanation: Ratification requires a principal in existence at the time of the act. A company cannot ratify what was done before it was born.

options.text: Neither the promoter nor the company is bound, the contract being void for want of a party
options.explanation: The promoter is bound. He contracted personally, whatever description he attached to his signature.

options.text: The promoter remains personally liable and the company can become bound only by entering into a fresh contract after incorporation
options.explanation: Correct. A pre-incorporation contract binds the promoters personally, cannot be ratified for want of a principal in existence, and reaches the company only through a fresh contract made after incorporation.

questions.stem: The Board of a company whose objects are confined to running a chain of bookshops acquires a fleet of tourist buses, and every member later approves the acquisition unanimously at a general meeting. The acquisition is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 4(1)(c); Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co Ltd v Riche

options.text: Valid, because the unanimous assent of every member cures any defect of authority
options.explanation: Unanimity cures an act beyond the ARTICLES or beyond the DIRECTORS' authority. It cannot confer on the company a capacity its memorandum never gave it.

options.text: Voidable at the option of the company, which may rescind it within a reasonable time
options.explanation: An ultra vires act is void, not voidable. There is no election to be made and no time limit to be observed.

options.text: Void as ultra vires the company, and incapable of ratification even by the unanimous vote of all the members
options.explanation: Correct. The objects clause fixes capacity, and Ashbury Railway Carriage v Riche holds that an act outside it is void and cannot be ratified; the directors are personally liable to restore the funds, and any member may seek an injunction.

options.text: Valid, because whatever a company's members unanimously want is fairly incidental to its objects
options.explanation: 'Fairly incidental' is an objective test about the connection between the act and the stated objects, not about what the members want.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Constructive notice and indoor management
questions.stem: Which statement about the doctrines of constructive notice and indoor management is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Royal British Bank v Turquand and its exceptions

options.text: Constructive notice protects the outsider and indoor management protects the company
options.explanation: The beneficiaries are the other way round: constructive notice protects the company, and the indoor-management rule protects the outsider dealing with it.

options.text: An outsider is deemed to know the contents of the memorandum and articles, but may presume that the internal procedure they require was duly followed
options.explanation: Correct. That is the balance the two doctrines strike, and the exceptions to Turquand's rule — knowledge of the irregularity, suspicious circumstances, forgery, no knowledge of the articles, and acts void in themselves — mark its limits.

options.text: The indoor-management rule protects a holder of a share certificate on which an officer's signature has been forged
options.explanation: A forged document is a nullity. There is no act of the company for the rule to regularise, so the holder takes nothing however innocent he is.

options.text: A director dealing with his own company may rely on the indoor-management rule like any other person
options.explanation: An insider is taken to know the internal position, so the knowledge exception ordinarily defeats him.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Separate personality and the veil · Case: Hemadri Steel
questions.case: Purnima holds 97 per cent of the shares of Hemadri Steel Private Limited and her son holds the remaining 3 per cent. Purnima is also employed by the company as its works manager under a written contract of service, on a salary fixed by the Board. Four matters arise in 2026. (i) The company defaults on ₹ 68,00,000 owed to a steel supplier, who sues Purnima personally on the footing that 'the company is really her'. (ii) Purnima is injured by a falling crane at the works and claims compensation as an employee; the insurer answers that a person who controls a company cannot be its employee. (iii) In 2023 Purnima had given a written undertaking to a former employer not to deal in alloy steel within 200 kilometres of Bhilai for five years; in June 2026 she registers Hemadri Alloys Private Limited, which she alone owns, and it at once begins dealing in alloy steel in Bhilai. (iv) On 1 March 2026 the son transfers his shares to Purnima, so that the company has one member; the company keeps trading and on 20 November 2026 takes an unsecured loan of ₹ 12,00,000 from a finance company, Purnima being fully aware of the position throughout.

readLink.label: Read: Separate legal entity in action →

questions.stem: On matter (i), the supplier's suit against Purnima personally will:
questions.sourceRef: s. 9; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd

options.text: Succeed, because a 97 per cent shareholder is in substance the company
options.explanation: Substance of that kind is what separate personality refuses to look at. Salomon itself concerned a founder who held all but six shares.

options.text: Fail, because the debt is the company's and Purnima's shareholding is no ground for lifting the veil
options.explanation: Correct. The company is a person distinct from its members and is not their agent or trustee; there is no fraud, no evasion of a pre-existing obligation and no statutory ground pleaded on these facts.

options.text: Succeed, because the company has become unable to pay and commercial failure is itself a ground for piercing
options.explanation: Insolvency is the risk creditors take. It is not fraud, and it is not one of the recognised grounds.

options.text: Fail, but only because the supplier did not obtain a personal guarantee from her
options.explanation: The absence of a guarantee is why the supplier has no separate contract with her, but the reason the suit fails is the company's separate personality, not a missing document.

questions.stem: On matter (ii), the insurer's answer that a controller cannot be an employee of her own company is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 9; Lee v Lee's Air Farming Ltd

options.text: Correct, because the same person cannot be both master and servant
options.explanation: She is not her own master. The employer is the company, a person distinct from her.

options.text: Correct, unless the Board resolution appointing her was passed in her absence
options.explanation: Procedural detail about the resolution goes to the validity of her appointment, not to whether a controlling member can be an employee at all.

options.text: Wrong, but only because she is a member and not a director of the company
options.explanation: The answer does not depend on which offices she holds. Even a governing director may be an employee of the company.

options.text: Wrong, because the company and Purnima are two distinct persons and the contract of service between them is valid
options.explanation: Correct. This is Lee v Lee's Air Farming: one person may at the same time be the controlling shareholder, the sole working director and an employee, because the contract is between two separate legal persons.

questions.stem: On matter (iii), the former employer's claim against Hemadri Alloys Private Limited will most likely:
questions.topic: Ch 6 · Lifting the veil · Evading an obligation
questions.sourceRef: Gilford Motor Co v Horne; Jones v Lipman

options.text: Succeed, the new company being a device or cloak to evade an obligation already binding on Purnima, so that an injunction runs against her and against it
options.explanation: Correct. The undertaking bound Purnima before the company existed, and the company was formed to do what she had promised not to do — the Gilford Motor v Horne pattern, applied in Jones v Lipman to a contract of sale.

options.text: Fail, because the company is a separate legal person which gave no undertaking
options.explanation: This states the rule without asking whether an exception applies. The timing — company formed after the obligation, to defeat it — is the exception.

options.text: Fail, because a restraint of trade covenant is void under s. 27 of the Indian Contract Act in every case
options.explanation: The question set is whether the corporate form can be used to escape the covenant; the covenant's own validity is a separate issue not raised by these facts.

options.text: Succeed only against Purnima, the company being immune as a separate person
options.explanation: Relief against her alone would be worthless, since the trading is done by the company. That is why the court reaches the company as well.

questions.stem: On matter (iv), the finance company's position in respect of the ₹ 12,00,000 loan is that:
questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 3A · Members below the minimum

options.text: The loan is void, the company having ceased to exist when its membership fell to one
options.explanation: Section 3A does not dissolve the company or invalidate its contracts. The company continues and remains liable.

options.text: Purnima is liable for one-half of the loan, jointly with the company
options.explanation: The section imposes SEVERAL liability for the WHOLE of the debts contracted during that time, not a proportionate share.

options.text: Purnima is severally liable for the whole ₹ 12,00,000, the six-month grace having expired on 1 September 2026 and she being cognisant of the shortfall
options.explanation: Correct. A private company needs two members; the shortfall began on 1 March 2026, the six months ran out on 1 September 2026, the loan was contracted on 20 November 2026 while the shortfall continued, and she knew of it.

options.text: Purnima is not liable at all, because the company was converted into a One Person Company on 1 March 2026
options.explanation: A private company does not become an OPC by a transfer of shares. An OPC is formed as such under s. 3(1)(c), or arrived at by the prescribed conversion process.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Classes of companies · Case: the Suvarna group
questions.case: Suvarna Holdings Limited is an unlisted PUBLIC company. Its position on 31 March 2026 is as follows. (i) It holds 7,20,000 of the 12,00,000 equity shares of Bhagirathi Metals Limited, each equity share carrying one vote; Bhagirathi has issued no other voting securities. (ii) Suvarna itself controls 34 per cent of the total voting power of Ratnagiri Alloys Private Limited, and Bhagirathi controls a further 19 per cent of Ratnagiri's total voting power; no one else holds more than 5 per cent. Ratnagiri's articles restrict the transfer of its shares, cap its members at two hundred and prohibit any invitation to the public, and it has 46 members. (iii) Suvarna controls 22 per cent of the total voting power of Chapala Foods Private Limited. Chapala's paid-up share capital is ₹ 3,90,00,000 and its turnover as per the profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year was ₹ 38,00,00,000. Chapala is not a holding or subsidiary company of anyone, is not registered under section 8 and is not governed by any special Act. All figures are to be tested on the position as on 28 February 2026.

questions.stem: In relation to Suvarna Holdings Limited, Bhagirathi Metals Limited is:

options.text: An associate, Suvarna's holding being significant but short of control
options.explanation: 7,20,000 of 12,00,000 votes is 60 per cent, which is more than one-half. The subsidiary test succeeds, and s. 2(6) excludes a subsidiary from being an associate.

options.text: A joint venture company, since Suvarna and the other shareholders share control
options.explanation: A joint venture needs a joint arrangement in which the parties have joint control and rights to the net assets. Suvarna controls Bhagirathi alone.

options.text: A subsidiary, Suvarna exercising 60 per cent of its total voting power, and Suvarna is accordingly its holding company
options.explanation: Correct. 7,20,000 of 12,00,000 votes is 60 per cent, which is more than one-half of the total voting power under s. 2(87)(ii); s. 2(46) then makes Suvarna the holding company.

options.text: Neither, because a public company cannot be the holding company of another public company
options.explanation: No such rule exists. Public companies routinely hold and are held by other public companies.

questions.stem: The percentage of Ratnagiri Alloys Private Limited's total voting power controlled by Suvarna Holdings Limited for the purposes of section 2(87)(ii), and the relationship it produces, are:
questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(87)(ii) · Control with a subsidiary
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(87)(ii) — 'either at its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies'

options.text: 53 per cent — Ratnagiri is a subsidiary of Suvarna, the clause allowing the holding company's own control to be added to that of its subsidiary
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(87)(ii) lets a company count voting power it exercises on its own together with that exercised by one or more of its subsidiaries. Bhagirathi is Suvarna's subsidiary, so 34 + 19 = 53 per cent, which is more than one-half.

options.text: 34 per cent — Ratnagiri is an associate of Suvarna, only a direct holding being relevant
options.explanation: This ignores the express words 'together with one or more of its subsidiary companies', which are in the clause precisely to prevent a group from splitting a holding to escape it.

options.text: 19 per cent — only Bhagirathi's holding is relevant, since Ratnagiri sits below it in the group
options.explanation: Bhagirathi's 19 per cent alone makes Ratnagiri neither its subsidiary nor even its associate; but the question is Suvarna's position, and Suvarna's own 34 per cent must be counted too.

options.text: 53 per cent — Ratnagiri is an associate of Suvarna, 53 per cent being at least 20 per cent
options.explanation: The arithmetic is right but the order of the tests is wrong. Section 2(6) applies only to a company that is NOT a subsidiary, and at 53 per cent the subsidiary test has already succeeded.

questions.stem: On the position as on 28 February 2026, Chapala Foods Private Limited is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(85) with the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules

options.text: Not a small company, because a company in which another company holds 22 per cent of the voting power is that company's subsidiary
options.explanation: 22 per cent is not more than one-half, so Chapala is not a subsidiary. It is an associate of Suvarna, which is a different thing.

options.text: Not a small company, because an associate company is one of the classes excluded by s. 2(85)
options.explanation: The three exclusions are a holding or subsidiary company, a s. 8 company, and a company governed by a special Act. An associate is not among them.

options.text: Not a small company, because its turnover of ₹ 38,00,00,000 exceeds the prescribed limit
options.explanation: The prescribed turnover limit is ₹ 40,00,00,000, and ₹ 38,00,00,000 does not exceed it.

options.text: A small company, its paid-up capital of ₹ 3,90,00,000 and turnover of ₹ 38,00,00,000 both being within the prescribed limits and none of the three exclusions applying
options.explanation: Correct. It is not a public company, capital of ₹ 3,90,00,000 is within ₹ 4,00,00,000, turnover of ₹ 38,00,00,000 is within ₹ 40,00,00,000, and being merely an associate is not an exclusion.

questions.stem: For the purposes of the Companies Act 2013, Ratnagiri Alloys Private Limited — whose articles remain those of a private company and whose name still ends in 'Private Limited' — is:
questions.topic: Ch 6 · s. 2(71) proviso · Deemed public company

options.text: A private company, because it has only 46 members and all three restrictions in its articles
options.explanation: Both facts are true and neither saves it. The proviso applies notwithstanding that the subsidiary continues to be a private company in its articles.

options.text: A public company, being a subsidiary of Suvarna Holdings Limited, which is not a private company
options.explanation: Correct. Ratnagiri is Suvarna's subsidiary on the 53 per cent computation, and Suvarna is a public company, so the proviso to s. 2(71) deems Ratnagiri public for the purposes of the Act.

options.text: A public company, but only from the date on which it alters its articles and changes its name
options.explanation: The deeming operates by force of the proviso from the moment the relationship exists; no alteration of articles or name is required, and the name may lawfully remain unchanged.

options.text: A private company, because the proviso applies only where the holding company is a listed company
options.explanation: The proviso says 'a company, not being a private company'. Listing is irrelevant; Suvarna is unlisted and the proviso still bites.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Incorporation and the doctrines · Case: Arunodaya Ceramics
questions.case: Devansh promoted Arunodaya Ceramics Private Limited, which was incorporated on 12 January 2026. Four matters arise. (i) On 3 December 2025, before incorporation, Devansh signed a contract 'for and on behalf of Arunodaya Ceramics Private Limited' with a kiln supplier for ₹ 15,00,000; on 20 January 2026 the Board resolved to ratify that contract, and the supplier has since delivered nothing and now sues the company. (ii) The memorandum confines the company's objects to the manufacture and sale of ceramic tiles. In March 2026 the Board, with the unanimous written approval of all four members recorded at a general meeting, spends ₹ 55,00,000 acquiring a fleet of taxis. (iii) The articles require any borrowing above ₹ 20,00,000 to be approved by an ordinary resolution of the members. In April 2026 the company borrows ₹ 30,00,000 from Meenakshi Finance on a document signed by two directors; no resolution was ever passed and Meenakshi did not know that. (iv) In May 2026 a clerk forges the managing director's signature on a share transfer form, and Meenakshi Finance is entered in the register of members as the holder of 2,000 shares.

questions.stem: On matter (i), the supplier's suit against the company will:

options.text: Succeed, because the Board's resolution of 20 January 2026 ratified the contract
options.explanation: Ratification needs a principal in existence when the act was done. On 3 December 2025 the company did not exist, so there was nothing capable of being ratified.

options.text: Succeed, because a promoter is the agent of the company he is forming
options.explanation: A promoter is not an agent; there is no principal yet. His position is fiduciary, which is a different relationship altogether.

options.text: Fail, and the supplier has no remedy against anyone, the contract being void
options.explanation: The contract is not void. Devansh contracted personally, whatever description he attached to his signature, and remains liable on it.

options.text: Fail against the company, Devansh remaining personally liable; the company can become bound only by a fresh contract made after incorporation
options.explanation: Correct. A pre-incorporation contract binds the promoters personally and cannot be ratified for want of a principal in existence; the company reaches it only through a fresh contract entered into after incorporation.

questions.stem: On matter (ii), the acquisition of the taxi fleet is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 4(1)(c); Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co Ltd v Riche

options.text: Valid, the unanimous approval of every member having cured the want of authority
options.explanation: Unanimity cures an act beyond the ARTICLES or beyond the DIRECTORS' authority. It cannot give the company a capacity the memorandum never conferred.

options.text: Valid, because operating taxis is fairly incidental to selling tiles, both involving transport
options.explanation: 'Fairly incidental' asks whether the act is a reasonable means of carrying out the stated objects. Running a taxi fleet is a separate business, not an incident of tile manufacture.

options.text: Void as ultra vires the company; the directors are personally liable to restore the ₹ 55,00,000, and any member may seek an injunction
options.explanation: Correct. The objects clause fixes capacity, an act outside it is void and cannot be ratified even unanimously (Ashbury v Riche), the directors must restore the funds applied ultra vires, and a member may sue to restrain further steps.

options.text: Voidable at the option of the company, which may rescind it within a reasonable time
options.explanation: An ultra vires act is void, not voidable. There is no election for the company to make.

questions.stem: On matter (iii), Meenakshi Finance's claim for repayment of the ₹ 30,00,000:
questions.sourceRef: Royal British Bank v Turquand; constructive notice

options.text: Fails, because the articles are a public document and Meenakshi is deemed to know that a members' resolution was required
options.explanation: Meenakshi is deemed to know the requirement, and that is where constructive notice stops. Whether the resolution was actually passed is an indoor matter it could not verify.

options.text: Succeeds, because Meenakshi was entitled to presume that the internal procedure required by the articles had duly been followed
options.explanation: Correct. This is Royal British Bank v Turquand: the outsider is bound by what the constitution says but may assume the internal steps it requires were taken, and none of the exceptions applies to Meenakshi on these facts.

options.text: Fails, because a borrowing beyond the limit in the articles is ultra vires the company and void
options.explanation: The borrowing is within the memorandum, so it is not ultra vires the COMPANY. Exceeding a limit in the articles is an internal irregularity, and the members could ratify it.

options.text: Succeeds only to the extent of ₹ 20,00,000, the limit the articles allowed without a resolution
options.explanation: The rule in Turquand's case validates the transaction as a whole against the company; it does not split the loan at the threshold in the articles.

questions.stem: On matter (iv), Meenakshi Finance's title to the 2,000 shares is:
questions.sourceRef: Exceptions to the rule in Turquand's case

options.text: No title at all, a forged document being a nullity, so that there is no act of the company for the indoor-management rule to regularise
options.explanation: Correct. Forgery is an established exception to Turquand's rule; it produces not an irregular company act but no company act whatever, and the innocence of the transferee cannot supply one.

options.text: Good title, since Meenakshi acted in good faith and may presume the internal procedure was followed
options.explanation: Good faith is not enough where the document is a forgery. The rule cures defects of internal procedure, not the absence of any genuine company act.

options.text: Good title, because the entry in the register of members is conclusive against the company
options.explanation: The register is evidence of membership, not a cure for a forged transfer; it may be rectified.

options.text: Good title, because the same lender succeeded on the borrowing in matter (iii)
options.explanation: The two matters turn on different points. A gap in internal procedure is curable by the rule; a forgery is one of its express exceptions.

questions.stem: State the characteristics of a company incorporated under the Companies Act 2013, and explain the present position of the common seal. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: The characteristics of a company →

skeleton.point: Corporate personality: on registration the company becomes a legal person distinct from its members and directors, capable of holding property, contracting, and suing and being sued in its own name
skeleton.citation: s. 9; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd

skeleton.point: Artificial legal person: created by law, with no physical existence, acting only through natural persons — the Board, officers and agents
Perpetual succession: existence unaffected by the death, insolvency or exit of members; the company continues until wound up or struck off
Limited liability: in a company limited by shares, the unpaid amount on the shares; in a guarantee company, the amount undertaken, payable only on winding up; no cap in an unlimited company
Separate property: company assets belong to the company, not to the members proportionately, so a member has no insurable interest in a particular company asset

Transferability of shares (freely transferable in a public company, restricted by the articles in a private company) and separation of ownership from management, the Board managing and the members owning

Common seal: OPTIONAL since the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015, so it is no longer a characteristic. Where a company has no seal, documents are signed by two directors, or by one director and the company secretary where one is appointed

questions.stem: Explain the doctrine of lifting the corporate veil, and state the statutory and judicial grounds on which the veil may be lifted. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: The rule first: a company is a legal person distinct from its members, so the members are prima facie not liable for its debts (Salomon). Lifting the veil is the EXCEPTION, applied where the corporate form is used as an instrument of fraud, evasion or improper conduct
skeleton.citation: s. 9; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd

skeleton.point: Statutory ground — members reduced below seven (public) or two (private) and business carried on for more than six months: every cognisant member severally liable for the whole of the debts contracted thereafter

Statutory grounds — incorporation obtained by false or incorrect information or by suppressing material facts; misstatement in a prospectus; fraudulent conduct of business in winding up; investigation into the persons really interested in the company
Judicial ground — protection of revenue, where a company exists only to reduce its controller's tax and the income returns to him as loans
Judicial grounds — fraud or improper conduct, and a company formed as a device or façade to evade an obligation already binding on its controller
skeleton.citation: Gilford Motor Co v Horne; Jones v Lipman

skeleton.point: Judicial grounds — determination of enemy character in wartime by looking at the nationality of those in control; avoidance of welfare or statutory liability; and the company acting genuinely as agent for its members
skeleton.citation: Daimler v Continental Tyre; Workmen of Associated Rubber Industry Ltd

questions.topic: Ch 6 · ss. 2(68), 2(71) · Private and public companies
