questions.stem: Distinguish between a private company and a public company under the Companies Act 2013, and explain when a private company is deemed to be a public company. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Definition of a private company: a company which by its ARTICLES restricts the right to transfer its shares, limits its members to two hundred, and prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities
Definition of a public company: a company which is not a private company. There is no minimum paid-up share capital for either, the fixed figures having been omitted in 2015

Counting rules inside the 200-member limb: joint holders count as one member; current employees who hold shares, and ex-employees who became members while employed and continued after leaving, are excluded; debenture-holders are not members at all

Points of distinction: minimum subscribers two versus seven; maximum members two hundred versus none; transfer restricted versus freely transferable; public invitation prohibited versus permitted; minimum directors two versus three; name ending 'Private Limited' versus 'Limited'

The deeming proviso: a company which is a subsidiary of a company that is not a private company is deemed to be a public company for the purposes of the Act, even where it continues to be a private company in its articles and keeps its 'Private Limited' name

questions.stem: Define a small company under the Companies Act 2013. State the tests it must satisfy, the companies to which the clause does not apply, and the relaxations small-company status carries. (5 marks)
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(85) with the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules

skeleton.point: Definition: a company, OTHER THAN a public company, which satisfies both the paid-up share capital test and the turnover test — so a public company can never be a small company however small it is

The two limbs are cumulative and are measured differently: paid-up share capital must not exceed the prescribed amount, and turnover AS PER THE PROFIT AND LOSS ACCOUNT FOR THE IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING FINANCIAL YEAR must not exceed the prescribed amount

The prescribed figures as on 28 February 2026 are ₹ 4,00,00,000 of paid-up share capital and ₹ 40,00,00,000 of turnover. They are set by RULES, not by the Act, and have already been raised twice, so they must be re-verified for the attempt

The clause does not apply at all to (A) a holding company or a subsidiary company, (B) a company registered under section 8, or (C) a company or body corporate governed by any special Act. The exclusions are absolute and are checked before the arithmetic
Relaxations: abridged annual return, only two board meetings in a year, no mandatory rotation of auditors, no cash flow statement in the financial statements, and lower monetary penalties

questions.stem: Define a holding company, a subsidiary company and an associate company under the Companies Act 2013, and explain the order in which the tests are applied. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Holding company: in relation to one or more other companies, a company of which such companies are subsidiary companies. The Explanation makes 'company' include any body corporate, so a foreign parent is covered

Subsidiary company: a company in which the holding company either (i) controls the composition of the Board of Directors, OR (ii) exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power, on its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies. The limbs are alternatives
Control of Board composition means the power, at the company's discretion, to appoint or remove all or a majority of the directors — a test that does not depend on shareholding at all
The base is TOTAL VOTING POWER, not total share capital, since the 2017 amendment; preference shares carrying votes only on resolutions directly affecting them are excluded from the voting base
Control exercised through another subsidiary counts: if A controls B and B controls C, C is a subsidiary of A. Percentages are never multiplied down the chain

Associate company: a company in which another company has significant influence but WHICH IS NOT A SUBSIDIARY, and includes a joint venture. Significant influence means control of at least twenty per cent of total voting power, or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement
Order of the tests, and the two comparators: subsidiary first (more than one-half), associate only if that fails (at least twenty per cent, so exactly twenty per cent qualifies)

questions.stem: Explain the doctrine of ultra vires and state its consequences for the company, its directors and a person who has lent money to it. (5 marks)
questions.sourceRef: s. 4(1)(c); Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co Ltd v Riche

skeleton.point: Meaning: 'ultra vires' means beyond the powers. The objects clause of the memorandum fixes the company's CAPACITY, and an act outside it is ultra vires the company and void

The leading case: a company whose objects were to make and sell railway carriages contracted to finance the construction of a railway line; the contract was ultra vires and void, and the later assent of every shareholder could not save it
skeleton.citation: Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co Ltd v Riche

skeleton.point: No ratification: an ultra vires act cannot be ratified even by the unanimous vote of all the members. Contrast an act beyond the ARTICLES or beyond the DIRECTORS' authority, which the members can ratify
The doctrine is applied reasonably: whatever is fairly incidental to or consequential upon the stated objects is intra vires

Consequences: any member may obtain an injunction to restrain a threatened ultra vires act; the directors are personally liable to restore the funds applied ultra vires and to compensate the company; and property acquired ultra vires nevertheless remains the company's property

The ultra vires lender: he cannot sue the company on a void loan, but equity allows him to TRACE his money or the property bought with it while identifiable, and to be SUBROGATED to a lawful creditor whose valid debt was discharged with it

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Classes of companies · Special classes
questions.stem: Write short notes on any four of the following: (a) One Person Company; (b) Government company; (c) foreign company; (d) section 8 company; (e) dormant company; (f) producer company. (5 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Dormant, Nidhi and producer companies →

skeleton.point: One Person Company: a company having only one person as a member; a species of private company formed under s. 3(1)(c); the memorandum names a nominee who, with prior written consent, becomes the member on the subscriber's death or incapacity; the 200-member limb is disapplied; relaxations include no annual general meeting and no cash flow statement

Government company: a company in which not less than 51 per cent of the PAID-UP SHARE CAPITAL is held by the Central Government, by any State Government or Governments, or partly by both, aggregated; and it includes a subsidiary of such a company

Foreign company: any company or body corporate incorporated outside India which has a place of business in India, by itself or through an agent, physically or in electronic mode, AND conducts any business activity in India in any other manner. Both limbs are required

Section 8 company: licensed by the Central Government where its objects are the promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity or protection of the environment, it applies its income only to those objects and prohibits any dividend; registered as a limited company without 'Limited' in its name; a firm may be a member; memorandum and articles alterable only with prior Central Government approval; never a small company

Dormant company: formed for a future project or to hold an asset or intellectual property and having no significant accounting transaction, or an inactive company; the status must be APPLIED FOR to the Registrar, who maintains a register of dormant companies. Payments of the Registrar's fees and for maintaining the office and records are not significant accounting transactions

Producer company: formed by ten or more individuals who are producers, or by two or more producer institutions, or a combination; objects around the production, pooling, grading, marketing and export of members' primary produce; membership confined to producers and shares not freely transferable; treated as a private company but without the 200-member cap
